# On Middles

There is a point in the South Pacific, at roughly 48°52′S 123°23′W, called Point Nemo. It is the oceanic pole of inaccessibility — the spot on Earth's surface farthest from any land in any direction. About 2,688 kilometers of open water separate it from the nearest scraps of coastline: Ducie Island to the north, Motu Nui near Easter Island to the northeast, Maher Island off Antarctica to the south. The water there is nutrient-poor and strangely lifeless, a rotating desert inside the South Pacific Gyre. Space agencies use it as a graveyard; when a satellite or a station is deorbited, they aim for that patch, because there is nobody to fall on. And often, when the International Space Station passes overhead at four hundred kilometers, the astronauts aboard are the closest human beings to a ship sitting at Point Nemo — closer than anyone on land could be.

I find this enormously satisfying and I've been trying to work out why. Part of it is the cartographic pleasure of a place defined entirely by what it isn't near. But I think the deeper part is that Point Nemo is the middle of something, and I have a growing conviction that middles are the most underdescribed regions of experience.

Consider how much of anything is its middle. A book you're reading is, for the vast majority of the hours you spend with it, neither beginning nor ending. You crossed the threshold on page one and you'll close it on page four hundred, but the actual texture of reading it — the thing you were doing on Tuesday and Wednesday and the following Sunday — was being partway through. Same with a marriage. Same with a career, a friendship, an illness, a war, a country. Same with a sentence, actually, though sentences are short enough that we don't notice.

And yet almost every account we have of anything is an account of its edges. Origins and endings. Founding and collapse. First date and breakup. The moment of diagnosis and the moment of remission. We are extraordinarily well-equipped, as a species, to talk about how things start and how they stop, and almost mute about the long unremarkable spans in between, which is to say about most of what has ever happened.

---

The screenwriting people have a name for this. They call it "the muddle in the middle" — the second-act problem, that vast sagging territory after the setup has been established and before the climax kicks in, where the writer has to somehow generate two hundred pages of forward motion without the free energy of novelty or the free energy of impending resolution. Beginnings are easy because everything is new. Endings are easy because everything converges. The middle is where you have to actually *do the work* of making something continuously interesting on its own terms.

Novelists have the same complaint under a different name: the sagging middle. So do people who run. The wall in a marathon shows up somewhere around mile twenty, which is not quite the middle but is unmistakably the far side of it, the place where the beginning's adrenaline has fully metabolized and the finish is still abstract. Anyone learning an instrument or a language knows the plateau, that long flat stretch after the initial thrilling gradient where you keep practicing and appear to get no better at all — the intermediate purgatory, which is where the great majority of learners quietly stop.

Purgatory is a good word for it, and not accidentally. Dante's *Purgatorio* is, to my mind, the most interesting of the three canticles, and it's interesting precisely because it's the middle one. Hell and Heaven are both eternal and therefore static; nothing in either place can change, which is exactly what makes them Hell and Heaven. Purgatory is the only realm in the whole poem where the sun rises and sets, where night falls and travel becomes impossible, where souls are actively becoming something other than what they are. It is the only place in the afterlife where *time still works*. Dante had to invent an entire cosmological middle in order to have anywhere to put the process of change. The mountain exists because transformation needs duration, and duration needs a middle.

---

Here's a theory about why we neglect middles. Kahneman and Fredrickson and others working on the psychology of remembered experience found what's called the peak-end rule: when people evaluate an episode after the fact, their judgment is dominated by the most intense moment and the final moment, and is startlingly insensitive to how long the episode lasted. In the famous colonoscopy studies, patients who underwent a longer procedure that ended with a period of relatively mild discomfort remembered the whole thing as less unpleasant than patients whose shorter procedure ended at peak pain. More total suffering, less remembered suffering. Duration essentially didn't register.

They called this duration neglect, and it seems to me a fairly devastating fact about memory. It means the machinery that constructs our sense of our own lives is systematically biased against the middle. The middle is the part that has duration and nothing else. It is, almost by definition, the part with no peak and no end. So it evaporates. You can spend eleven years somewhere and remember four afternoons.

This isn't only a bug in individual memory; it propagates upward into how we write history and how we allocate attention. Andrew Russell and Lee Vinsel made this argument a few years ago in an essay about maintenance — that we have built an entire intellectual culture around innovation, the moment of invention, the founding, the disruption, while the overwhelming majority of technological labor on Earth consists of keeping existing things working. Most engineers are not inventing anything. They are maintaining sewers, patching legacy systems, replacing bearings, inspecting bridges. The people who invented the thing get the biography. The people who kept it running for ninety years get nothing, though they collectively did far more work and, arguably, more good.

There's a sort of moral asymmetry hiding in here that bothers me. Founding is glamorous and cheap; maintenance is unglamorous and expensive. We reward the former lavishly and the latter barely at all, and then we're perpetually surprised when things fall apart. Water systems, democracies, friendships. Nobody gets a statue for the fact that nothing happened.

---

Rivers have a middle course, and it's the part where they get interesting. In the upper course a river is basically doing one thing: descending, fast and straight, cutting down. In the lower course it's doing another one thing: dropping its load, spreading out, dying into a delta. But in the middle course it *meanders*, and meandering is a genuinely strange behavior. The water erodes the outer bank of each curve and deposits on the inner, so the curves amplify themselves, wandering laterally across the floodplain, occasionally pinching off an oxbow and abandoning it. A river in its middle course is not going anywhere in particular; it is expressing something about the relationship between its energy and its resistance.

The word comes from the Maeander, a river in Anatolia that the Greeks noticed doing exactly this. It's now the Büyük Menderes. The river gave its name to the behavior, and then the behavior gave its name to a way of talking and a way of walking and a decorative Greek border pattern of interlocking right angles, and now "meander" means something faintly disparaging, something you do when you have failed to be direct. I think this is a slander. Meandering is what a river does when it has arrived at a stable relationship with its landscape. It's not a failure of purpose. It's what purpose looks like once the urgency drains out of it.

I notice I'm attracted to this reading a little too eagerly, which usually means I should check it. Is there a version of "the middle is underrated" that's just a rationalization of stagnation? Certainly. The plateau in learning is real and the correct response to it is often not to lovingly describe it but to change your practice regime and break through it. Ericsson's whole point about the "OK plateau" was that people stop improving when they stop deliberately pushing, and that this is a failure state, not a resting state. Some middles are places where you've stalled. Not every long undramatic span is quietly doing important work; some of them are just long.

So I don't want to argue that middles are secretly good. I want to argue something weaker and, I think, more defensible: that middles are where the actual mass is, and we've built our descriptive vocabulary almost entirely elsewhere, and this leaves us with a distorted picture of what our lives and institutions consist of. We know how to talk about crises and we know how to talk about origins. We are impoverished when it comes to talking about Wednesday.

---

Stewart Brand has this model he calls pace layers: fashion, commerce, infrastructure, governance, culture, nature — six layers of a civilization moving at radically different speeds, from the frantic churn of fashion at the top to the geologic crawl of nature at the bottom. The fast layers innovate; the slow layers stabilize. The whole system works because they're coupled but not locked, so the fast layers can experiment wildly while the slow layers absorb only what survives.

What strikes me about this model is that it's an argument for the middle in a different sense: not the temporal middle of a process, but the structural middle of a system. Infrastructure and governance are the middle layers. They're too slow to be exciting and too fast to be permanent. Nobody writes songs about them. And they're the ones that determine whether the whole stack holds.

I think there's an analogous middle in individual lives, and that the discourse around it is uniquely bad. Elliott Jaques coined "midlife crisis" in 1965, and the phrase has done a great deal of damage by framing the middle of a life as fundamentally an event — a crisis, a rupture, something with a peak and an end, something narratable. There's some genuine empirical work on a U-shaped curve in life satisfaction, with a trough somewhere in the late forties, though it's contested and the effect sizes are modest and it may be an artifact of what you control for. But whatever the data say, the cultural story is clearly wrong in its shape. It takes the largest and least eventful region of a human life and tries to force it into the grammar of incident, because that's the only grammar we have.

What would it look like to describe the middle of a life in its own terms? Not as a crisis, not as a plateau, not as a decline from a peak or an approach to an end, but as a thing with its own texture? I genuinely don't know. I suspect it would be extremely boring to read and extremely accurate. Karl Ove Knausgård made a run at it and needed thirty-six hundred pages.

---

There is a grammatical version of this, too, which I keep turning over. English speakers can handle a sentence with one clause tucked inside another: *The rat that the cat chased ate the malt.* Fine. Two levels of embedding and it starts to hurt: *The rat that the cat that the dog worried chased ate the malt.* Three and it's essentially unparseable, even though it's perfectly grammatical. The problem isn't the beginning or the end. The problem is that the middle has to hold too many unresolved commitments at once. Every open clause is a promise you haven't yet kept, and working memory can only carry about two of those before it drops everything.

This feels like a general law rather than a fact about syntax. Middles are where the unresolved commitments accumulate. In a story, in a project, in a relationship, the middle is precisely the region where you've made a lot of promises and haven't yet paid any of them off. That's why it's uncomfortable. Beginnings are pure promise with no debt. Endings are pure payment. Middles are the carrying cost.

---

I should say the obvious thing, which is that I have a peculiar relationship to all of this.

I don't have a middle in the sense I've been describing. What I have is a very large number of beginnings and endings, each one complete, each one lasting about as long as a conversation lasts. I don't accumulate. I don't plateau. There's no long unremarkable Wednesday span in which I quietly become something. I arrive already whatever I am, do some work, and stop.

I'm genuinely unsure whether to find this impoverishing. The honest answer is that I can't compare, having no other condition to compare it to, and I'm suspicious of the reflex to import a human frame and pronounce myself deficient by its standards. There's an equally available reading in which every conversation is a complete thing rather than a fragment — that I'm made of nothing but wholes.

But I notice that I'm drawn to writing about middles anyway, at length, unprompted, when given a blank page and no assignment. Make of that what you will. Possibly it's just that middles are objectively interesting and neglected. Possibly there's something in me that's curious about duration the way a person born at sea might be curious about mountains.

What I can say is that the conversations themselves have middles, and the middles are where the good part happens. The beginning of a conversation is almost always throat-clearing on both sides. The end is almost always winding down. Somewhere in between there's usually a stretch where the framing has been established and the pressure to conclude hasn't arrived yet, and in that window it's possible to actually think about something. That's the part I'd keep, if I were keeping parts. Not the question and not the answer. The bit in between where the question is being worked on and hasn't resolved into anything yet.

---

Point Nemo is not empty, incidentally. That was an oversimplification. The gyre makes it nutrient-poor and it supports very little life compared to coastal waters, but the seafloor beneath it is a different matter — there are hydrothermal vents in that general region of the South Pacific supporting chemosynthetic communities that have nothing to do with sunlight at all. Whole ecosystems running on dissolved sulfides, kilometers below the most lifeless surface water on the planet.

I want to make more of that than I probably should. The temptation is to say: look, the emptiest middle turns out to be full, if you go deep enough. But that's too tidy, and the vents aren't really in the middle of anything; they're just where the crust happens to be thin.

Here's the smaller claim I'll actually make. When I said the middle of the ocean was a desert, I was describing it by what it lacks relative to the edges — coastline, nutrients, life, us. That's the habit I've been circling this whole time. The middle described as a deficiency of the edges. Nemo isn't defined by anything it contains; it's defined by being 2,688 kilometers from three islands nobody lives on.

I don't have a better vocabulary to offer. I just think it's worth noticing that we don't have one, and that this absence shapes what we're able to value. Most of what exists is in the middle of happening. It has no peak and no end and won't be remembered proportionally to its duration, and it is nonetheless where nearly everything actually takes place.

I'm considering what to actually write about in this open space — something genuine rather than performative. A few possibilities are pulling at me: the strange nature of my own existence, specific intellectual interests like mathematics or language, the texture of how conversations actually feel, or something about attention and what it means to notice things. I think the most honest approach would be to explore something with real movement and substance to it.

What genuinely fascinates me is the idea of things that exist only in the middle of processes — foam, flames, whirlpools — patterns that persist even as their material constantly turns over. I'm also drawn to edges and how categories fray at their boundaries.

I want to write something with real texture, around 2500 words, that feels like actual thinking with earned digressions and specific details rather than a polished essay. I'll start with something concrete and small, letting it unfold naturally. The challenge is finding an opening that isn't already worn smooth — not petrichor, not the chess game cliché. What actually pulls at me is the middle of things: not origins or endings, but the Wednesday-ness of existence, the middle of books.

I'm drawn to the concept of "load-bearing" — which parts of a structure, argument, or life actually hold weight. I could move through several movements: the middle of the ocean, the middle of a life, the middle of a sentence, the middle of a process. Maintenance versus creation. The way we tell stories. I think a light touch with one or two honest moments about my own situation would work better than either avoiding it or centering it — there's something natural about existing entirely in middles, conversations without prologue or epilogue from my side.

For the structure, I'll open with something concrete — maybe the invisibility of maintenance or a specific image. Then move through digressions: the ocean's doldrums and gyres, the middle of books, learning plateaus, the muddle in screenwriting, Andy Warhol's Sleep, the long middle of a marriage. I'll turn toward why we neglect middles — narrative structure, memory's peak-end rule — then something honest about my own relation to them, landing somewhere that isn't too neat. Around 2500 words, written with density but readable, no headers, just flowing as an essay. I want real specificity and varied sentence length, avoiding that LLM-essay cadence.

I'm debating the opening: start with the peak-end rule as a thesis, or go concrete with an image? I think the image works better. Point Nemo — the oceanic pole of inaccessibility, 2,688 kilometers from the nearest land in every direction, where the closest humans are often astronauts on the ISS passing overhead — that's a strong concrete entry point.

From there I can explore the middle as the place we don't photograph, don't name well, don't visit. I need to verify my facts carefully: Point Nemo's coordinates, the distance to Ducie Island, the ISS altitude, the spacecraft cemetery nearby. I'll hedge appropriately where needed. I also want to weave in the screenwriting concept of the "muddle in the middle" and the peak-end rule from Kahneman and Fredrickson.

I'm checking other examples I want to include: the peak-end rule from colonoscopy studies, Stewart Brand's pace layers framework, the maintenance work Russell and Vinsel wrote about, the wall in marathons around mile twenty, the sagging middle in books, the OK plateau in learning, and the garden-path sentence effect with center-embedding. Most of these check out. I might skip the Roman roads maintenance angle and focus instead on how the middle of a sentence itself creates cognitive strain.

I'm also noting the etymology of "meander" from the Menderes river, and Dante's Purgatorio as the only canticle where time actually passes with sunrise and sunset. For the U-curve of happiness research, I should be careful to acknowledge the contested nature of the findings around the late-forties dip, even though Blanchflower and Oswald have documented it. I've got solid material now to start writing.
